newsitem.title: INDIA: India relaxes rules on firms' overseas investments.
newsitem.headline: India relaxes rules on firms' overseas investments.

text.p: The Indian government on Friday relaxed rules governing overseas investment by domestic firms in a move that analysts described as a bid to use the nation's foreign exchange reserves efficiently.
The new steps were designed to encourage Indian firms to expand overseas and help the country move towards capital account convertibility of the rupee, the Finance Ministry said in a statement.
"The measures are aimed at prudent utilisation of foreign exhange reserves," Vipin Aggarwal, chief dealer at DBS Capital Trust Securities India Pvt Ltd, told Reuters.
India's foreign exchange reserves have risen to $28.22 billion on June 6 compared with $21.66 billion a year earlier.
"The cost of maintaining foreign exchange is high," Aggarwal said.

The ministry said Indian companies raising funds through Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs), or equity offerings overseas, could now mobilise up to 50 percent of the value of the offering through investment in foreign ventures.
It did not say what the earlier, lower investment limit was.
Indian companies which have subsidiaries or joint ventures overseas can raise money overseas and use the funds to increase their competitiveness in the global market, Aggarwal said.
"It is up to the Indian companies to utilise this facility," he said.
"They have implemented some minor recommendations of the report on capital account convertibility," said an economist with a foreign securities firm, who asked not to be identified.
A committee appointed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the country's central bank, earlier this month unveiled an ambitious road-map for the rupee's full convertibility by the year 2000.
The RBI, which was earlier empowered to approve Indian firms' investment proposals valued at up to $10 million, can now clear plans for up to $15 million, the finance ministry said.
"The impact of the measures on the foreign exchange reserves can be delayed and there will be a lag effect," an economist with a foreign securities firm said.
